opus-5.5.text:
Well, because it's the piece that actually gets you something neither side of the field has on its own. The first half of the paper shows that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are essentially the same thing. A Datalog rule is a join followed by a projection, and that's exactly what a tensor contraction does. So you can write symbolic AI and neural networks in one language. That's nice, but in a sense it's a unification of notation. The embedding-space reasoning is where the unification starts paying for itself.

Here's the idea. Instead of representing objects as one-hot symbols, you represent them as embedding vectors, and relations become tensors built out of those embeddings. Then you run the same logical rules, the same contractions, but now over the embeddings. What you get has a temperature knob, if you like. At zero temperature, with the embeddings nearly orthogonal, you recover pure deductive logic. It's sound, it's transparent, and it doesn't hallucinate, because it can only conclude what actually follows. As you raise the temperature, similar objects start borrowing inferences from each other. Now you're doing analogical reasoning and generalization, which is the thing neural networks are good at and logic is terrible at.

So for the first time you have a single system where you can dial between rigorous deduction and fuzzy, similarity-based generalization, and you can do it in a principled way rather than bolting a neural net onto a theorem prover. Getting both reliability and learnability out of one mechanism is, I think, what AI has been missing. LLMs give you generalization, but you can't trust the reasoning. Classical symbolic AI gives you trustworthy reasoning, but it's brittle and doesn't learn well. Reasoning in embedding space is the bridge. That's why I think it's the most important part, and frankly the part I'm most eager to see people take further.

r001.rationale: The response says near-orthogonal embeddings recover deduction, but does not state that random embeddings enable pure logical deduction.

r002.rationale: It says similar objects can borrow inferences as temperature rises, but does not explain that training brings embeddings closer for objects with similar inferences.

r003.rationale: It identifies zero temperature with pure deduction, but does not connect that limit to TensorLogic’s sigmoid nonlinearity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, because it's the thing that neither symbolic AI nor neural networks could do on their own, and it's the thing that, frankly, I've been chasing for most of my career.

Think about what we have today. On one side you have symbolic reasoning, which is sound. If the premises are true and you apply the rules correctly, the conclusions are true. But it's brittle. It can't handle noise, it can't generalize beyond exactly what you wrote down, and it falls apart the moment the world doesn't match your predicates. On the other side you have deep learning, which generalizes beautifully, handles ambiguity, learns from data, but it can't actually reason. Large language models hallucinate because there's nothing in the architecture that forces the output to follow from the input. They're doing something that looks like reasoning, but there's no guarantee behind it.

What TensorLogic does, at the core, is notice that a logical rule and an Einstein summation are the same operation. A Datalog rule that joins relations and projects out variables is literally a tensor contraction, if you represent relations as Boolean tensors. Once you see that, the whole distinction between logic and neural networks collapses. They're both just tensor equations.

And here's the part I find exciting. Once the relations are tensors, the objects don't have to be discrete symbols anymore. They can be embeddings. You can take the same rule, "if X is a parent of Y and Y is a parent of Z, then X is a grandparent of Z," and apply it not to a lookup table of names but to vectors in a continuous space. The reasoning happens over similarities. So you get the generalization of embeddings, where things that are alike get treated alike, while the structure of the inference is still the logical rule. You didn't lose the chain of reasoning. You can still inspect it.

And crucially, you have a knob. There's a temperature parameter, and when you turn it to zero you recover exact deductive reasoning, with no hallucination, because the system can only derive what follows from the rules. When you turn it up, you get analogical reasoning, where the system will say "this is close enough to something I know, so probably the same conclusion applies." That's what humans do. We reason deductively when we can and by analogy when we have to, and we move between the two fluidly. Nobody has had a single mechanism that does both before.

So that's why I think this is the heart of it. The unification of all the architectures into one language is nice, and the efficiency is nice, and being able to write transformers in a few lines is nice. But reasoning in embedding space is a genuinely new capability. It's the piece that could get us from systems that merely sound intelligent to systems that actually are, in a way we can trust and understand.

r001.rationale: The response says TensorLogic can reason over embeddings, but does not state that it can perform pure deduction using random embeddings.

r002.rationale: It says similar objects are treated alike, but does not explain that training brings vectors closer for objects that tend to produce the same inferences.

r003.rationale: It links zero temperature to exact deduction, but does not identify this as the zero-temperature limit of TensorLogic’s sigmoid nonlinearity.

astra-6.text:
Because it opens up the possibility of combining what neural networks do well with what symbolic reasoning does well at a much deeper level. Neural networks are very good at learning representations. Symbolic systems are very good at composing rules and drawing conclusions. The challenge is getting those capabilities to work together.

In embedding space, a concept is represented by a vector rather than just a discrete symbol. That gives you similarity and generalization: two things can be related even if they don’t have exactly the same name or satisfy exactly the same predicate. But we also want to perform structured reasoning with those representations—to carry out a sequence of inferences, rather than just recognize a pattern.

The exciting possibility with TensorLogic is that you can express those reasoning operations in the same mathematical language as the neural computation. You don’t have to learn a representation, translate it into a separate symbolic system, reason there, and then translate back. The reasoning can operate directly on the learned representations.

Now, that doesn’t mean an arbitrary operation on embeddings suddenly becomes valid logical inference. You still have to specify what the operations mean. But it gives us a framework for bringing learning and reasoning together. To me, that’s the big opportunity: systems that can learn the concepts they need and then reason with those concepts.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning can operate directly on learned representations, but does not state that TensorLogic performs pure logical deduction using random embeddings.

r002.rationale: It discusses similarity and generalization in embedding space, but does not explain that training moves vectors closer for objects that tend to receive the same inferences.

r003.rationale: The response mentions no sigmoid nonlinearity, temperature, or zero-temperature limit.

sol-6.1.text:
Because that’s where learning and reasoning can really come together. Neural networks learn these rich representations of the world in embedding spaces, but traditional symbolic reasoning operates on discrete symbols. So you have this gap: the system that learns doesn’t naturally speak the same language as the system that reasons.

The exciting possibility with TensorLogic is that you can express logical operations in the same framework that you use for neural computation. Reasoning doesn’t have to wait until you’ve converted everything into symbols and thrown away much of the information in the representation. You can reason with those representations themselves.

Think about analogy. We often draw an inference because two situations have a similar structure, even though the objects involved are different. You want a system that can exploit that similarity while also composing several steps of reasoning. Embeddings give you a way to capture similarity; logic gives you a way to compose inferences.

To me, that’s the big opportunity: learning representations that make reasoning easier, and using reasoning to guide what gets learned. They become parts of the same process.
